loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
question: A member of the board risk committee of a US university endowment is reading a report from the endowment’s USD equity manager explaining why modeling transaction costs forces the manager to be more precise about its alphas. Which of the following statements in the report is LEAST accurate?

options.A: When only alpha and active risk are considered, a mis-scaled set of alphas can be offset by raising or lowering active risk aversion.
options.B: Once transaction costs are included, precision matters most in the covariance estimates, because costs are traded off against active risk rather than against alpha.
options.C: Once transaction costs are included, a second trade-off, between alpha and transaction costs, sits alongside the trade-off between alpha and active risk.
options.D: Including transaction costs increases the importance of both precise alpha estimates and the correct choice of alpha scale.

solution:
Endowment board member checks a manager’s report on why costs force alpha precision; find the least accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 4.4 gives the reasoning in three steps. First, with only alphas and active risk, “we can offset any problem in setting the scale of the alphas by increasing or decreasing the active risk aversion”; it is a one-dimensional problem with a single knob. Second, “transactions costs make this a two-dimensional problem. The trade-off between alpha and active risk remains, but now there is a new trade-off between the alpha and the transactions costs.” Third, “we therefore must be precise in our choice of scale, to correctly trade off between the hypothetical alphas and the inevitable transactions costs”; costs “force greater precision on our estimate […]

loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
question:
A portfolio manager at a London multi-manager firm has capital for one more GBP position in a FTSE 350 mandate. All four candidates have the same marginal contribution to active risk, and each can be replaced at the end of its holding period by a similar successor, so each annualized figure applies throughout the year.

| Trade | Alpha (% per year) | Round-trip cost (%) | Holding (months) | Free float (GBP bn) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K | 6.80 | 2.40 | 3 | 4.1 |
| L | 5.40 | 0.90 | 3 | 12.6 |
| M | 4.00 | 1.20 | 24 | 2.3 |
| N | 2.60 | 0.30 | 9 | 18.9 |

Which trade adds the most annual alpha net of amortized transaction costs?

options.A: Trade K
options.B: Trade L
options.C: Trade M
options.D: Trade N

solution:
London PM ranks four GBP trades by alpha net of amortized costs; free float is irrelevant.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s two-stock example makes one point that this question generalizes: the best trade is not the one with the highest alpha or the lowest cost, but the one with the highest alpha net of annualized cost, because the annual cost depends on how often the round trip is paid. In GARP’s example both stocks have the same 4% annual alpha, yet the 24-month hold earns 3.25% a year and the 6-month rotation only 1%. With equal marginal contributions to active risk, ranking by

$\alpha- \frac{\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}}{\text{h}}$

is the right comparison, and it is where the alpha versus cost trade-off of GARP 4.4 becomes concrete.

question:
A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund runs an AUD 1.4 billion active equity mandate. After new research she revises the alpha of stock K. The portfolio was optimal before the revision, with no limits on holdings or cash and no other constraints. Her inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Revised alpha of K, $\alpha_{\text{K}}$ (%) | 2.10 |
| Active risk aversion, $\lambda_{\text{A}}$ | 0.06 |
| Portfolio active risk, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ (%) | 4.00 |
| Marginal contribution of K to active risk, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{K}}$ | 1.50 |
| Purchase cost, $\text{PC}_{\text{K}}$ (%) | 0.60 |
| Sales cost, $\text{SC}_{\text{K}}$ (%) | 0.85 |
| Benchmark weight of K (%) | 3.20 |

Which of the following gives the correct action on stock K and its net benefit at the margin?

options.A: Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 0.78%.
options.B: Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 0.53%.
options.C: Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 1.38%.
options.D: Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 1.14%.

solution:
Australian superannuation PM revises stock K’s alpha; correct action and net benefit at the margin?

**Concept and theory**

Transaction costs create a gap between “worth holding more” and “worth paying to hold more”. Buying stock n costs $\text{PC}_{\text{n}}$ per unit traded; the benefit per unit is $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$. So a purchase is justified only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} > \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$, and its net benefit at the margin is $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} - \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$. Symmetrically, selling saves $-\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ per unit and costs $\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, so a sale is justified only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} < -\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, with net benefit $-\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} - \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$. A junior risk analyst at a São Paulo asset manager is preparing a rebalancing report for a BRL equity fund and must state the alpha no-trade band for stock M, a current holding. The fund’s portfolio is optimal, with no limits on holdings or cash. The inputs are:

|---|---|

| Portfolio active risk, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ (%) | 6.00 |

| Purchase cost, $\text{PC}_{\text{M}}$ (%) | 0.45 |

He receives a revised alpha for stock R.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Information ratio, IR | 0.60 |
| Target (and current) active risk, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ (%) | 4.00 |
| Marginal contribution of R to active risk, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{R}}$ | 0.90 |
| Purchase cost, $\text{PC}_{\text{R}}$ (%) | 0.40 |
| Sales cost, $\text{SC}_{\text{R}}$ (%) | 0.55 |
| Benchmark weight of R (%) | 1.80 |
| Revised alpha of R, $\alpha_{\text{R}}$ (%) | 1.10 |

Which statement about stock R’s alpha no-trade band and the right response is correct?

options.A: The band is −0.01% to 0.94%; the revised alpha calls for buying more of R.
options.B: The band is 0.53% to 1.48%; the revised alpha calls for no trade in R.
options.C: The band is 0.14% to 1.09%; the revised alpha calls for buying more of R.

question: The CIO of a Japanese corporate pension fund sets a static 70/30 equity/bond target for its JPY 120 billion portfolio. Following Leland (1996), and assuming linear transaction costs and a utility function that penalizes variance relative to the target and transaction costs over time, the fund’s no-trade region for the equity weight is 66% to 74%. After a rally the equity weight reaches 77%. Which action and consequence are consistent with Leland’s result?

options.A: Sell equities back to the 70% target, because once the region is breached the optimal trade restores the target allocation in full.
options.B: Make no trade until the next scheduled quarterly review, and then sell equities back to the 70% target allocation at that date.
options.C: Sell equities down to 74%, the nearest boundary; this cuts turnover and costs roughly in half with effectively no change in risk over time.

- The optimal strategy has a **no-trade region** around the target.
- If the portfolio moves outside the region, trade **back to the boundary**, not to the target.

Which of the following statements in the summary is least accurate?

Leland’s no-trade region (see Q10) is a band in allocation space. GARP adds three points about it. (1) Drivers: its size depends on the transaction costs, the risk aversion, and the expected return and risk of stocks and bonds. (2) Turnover: changing the size of the region changes the strategy’s turnover; a wider region is breached less often and so trades less. (3) Scope: the problem solved is one-dimensional and involves no flow of information (the target is static), so it is much simpler than general active management; still, it motivates boundary-driven rather than purely calendar-driven rebalancing rules.

loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
question:
Richard Cryer, FRM, is a fund manager in New York. During a workshop with junior managers, he made the following comments:

I. The correct way to compare transactions costs incurred on the annual rate of gain from alpha and the annual rate of loss from active risk is to amortize the transactions costs where the rate of amortization depends on the anticipated holding period.

II. The annualized transactions cost is given by round trip cost divided by the holding period in years.

options.A: Only I is correct
options.B: Only II is correct
options.C: Both I and II are correct
options.D: Both I and II are incorrect

solution:
**Concept**

Transactions costs are paid at a point in time, while alpha and active risk are annual rates. To compare them, the cost must be amortised over the expected holding period: annualised transactions cost $= \frac{\text{round-trip cost}}{\text{holding period in years}}$ .

**Exam trap.** A longer holding period lowers the annualised cost, which is why high-turnover strategies need much larger alphas to pay for themselves.

loText: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs.
question:
A portfolio manager currently holds stock QYZ and is deciding whether to increase, decrease, or maintain the position based on new information. The manager gathers the following inputs:

- Alpha for stock QYZ (αQYZ): 0.25
- Marginal contribution to active risk (MCAR) for stock QYZ: 0.17
- Active risk (ψ): 2.3
- Active risk aversion (λA): 0.32
- Cost to purchase stock QYZ: 0.30%
- Cost to sell stock QYZ: 0.40%

The manager calculates the marginal contribution to value added (MCVA) for the stock and uses this metric to determine the appropriate action to take. Which of the following is the best action for the manager to take and the explanation for this action?

options.A: Purchase more of stock QYZ because its MCVA is greater than the purchase cost.
options.B: Purchase more of stock QYZ because the MCVA is greater than its MCAR.
options.C: Sell the position in stock QYZ because its MCVA is negative.
options.D: Maintain the position in stock QYZ because its MCVA is greater than the negative of the sales cost.

solution:
**Concept**

With transactions costs there is a no-trade region. Marginal contribution to value added: MCVA = $\alpha- 2 \lambda_{A} \psi$ MCAR. Buy if MCVA exceeds the purchase cost; sell if MCVA is below the negative of the sales cost; otherwise hold: $-\text{SC} \le\text{MCVA} \le$ PC.

**Working**

MCVA = 0.25 − 2 × 0.32 × 2.3 × 0.17 = 0.25 − 0.2502 = −0.02%

**No-trade band:** from −0.40% (negative of the sales cost) to +0.30% (purchase cost).

−0.40% \< −0.02% \< 0.30%, so the position is inside the band.

**Exam trap.** A negative MCVA is not by itself a reason to sell. The loss from holding has to exceed the cost of selling.

loText: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the following portfolio construction techniques: screens, stratification, linear programming, and quadratic programming.
question: Which of the following statements regarding the various portfolio construction techniques is correct?

options.A: Although screening ignores all information in alphas except the rankings, it limits transaction costs through judicious choice of the buy, sell, and hold lists.
options.B: The stratification technique provides superior risk control by overweighting the categories with lower risks and underweighting the categories with higher risks.
options.C: The linear programming approach characterizes stocks along dimensions of risk, and requires that these dimensions distinctly and exclusively partition the stocks.
options.D: Quadratic programming requires many more inputs than other portfolio construction techniques and as a result minimizes both noise and the potential for poor calibration.

solution:
**Concept**

Four portfolio construction techniques. Screens: rank by alpha and buy the top names; simple, uses only the rankings, crude risk control. Stratification: hold stocks in each category in line with the benchmark’s weights. Linear programming: characterise stocks along several risk dimensions and keep the portfolio close to the benchmark on each. Quadratic programming: uses alphas, risks and transactions costs together, but needs the most inputs.

**Exam trap.** Each wrong option gives one technique the defining feature of another, or reverses the consequence of having many inputs.

loText: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the following portfolio construction techniques: screens, stratification, linear programming, and quadratic programming.

**Concept**

Same four techniques, judged on risk control. Screens: fragmentary risk control. Stratification: risk controlled by matching benchmark weights by category. Linear programming: stays close to the benchmark on many risk dimensions. Quadratic programming: models risk explicitly with volatilities and all pairwise correlations, at the cost of many more estimated inputs.
